notes.AS04: This passage shows grief at its most open: Jacob mourns his son for many days and will not accept comfort from anyone. It speaks to the crushing part of what you wrote, since the passage gives no measure for how heavily or how long a person may mourn. It says nothing about a parent who was unkind, or about guilt, so it doesn't reach that part.
notes.AS06: The passage doesn't speak to relief at all; it is a child watching her mother vanish and feeling regret, weakness and tears. It does speak to the other side of what you wrote: the loss of a mother, and the grief of a parting that can't be undone. The passage says "the first step, parting me from my mother, was taken," and it stays with that parting without judging the one who feels it.
notes.AS07: The passage speaks to the part of your wish to be there for her, and not to the question of checking in or giving space. What it says about being with someone grieving is to accommodate yourself to her in conversation, even to groan with her if need be. It also says not to be overcome by her sorrow yourself, which may bear on your worry about saying something wrong.
notes.AS12: The passage speaks to one part of what you wrote: feeling lonely while sitting right beside someone. Thoreau says we are often lonelier "among men" than alone in a room, and that solitude isn't measured by the distance between people. He says nothing about marriage or what companionship is supposed to feel like, only that closeness in space and loneliness can exist together.
notes.AS14: The passage speaks to the part of what you wrote about how he treated you badly. It says that thinking "they did wrong to me, but what can I possibly do?" is how resentment gets dropped. It says nothing about checking his accounts or about waiting, so it speaks only to the wrong done to you.
notes.AS16: The passage is about wrongs done by a brother, so it touches your situation only at the point where your sister is concerned, not your parents' blame or their screaming. It says an unfair thing can be held by a handle that cannot be carried, and it names holding on to the other person's injustice as that handle. Its counsel is to hold instead to the fact that she is family, raised alongside you.
notes.AS20: The passage speaks to the part of your situation where your sister called you selfish, since it is about setting your own interests aside for others and doing so even when your nature rebels. It says this love is asked of God, and that the rest is left to Him. It does not speak to the move itself or to how you keep your family close, only to the cost of giving way.
notes.AS21: The passage says that what is finest in a life, the clothes, the meal, the bed, comes from other people's hands and homes, and it asks how anyone could separate from them. That lines up with your sense of owing your family everything: it describes receiving much from others. It doesn't speak to how to become independent or to your mother's question about what will happen to her.
notes.AS28: This passage is spoken by someone cut off from friends, and it puts her situation into words: being left out, shut in, and eyes dim with grief. It says nothing about how to comfort someone in that place, so it doesn't answer your question about what to say. What it does hold is the picture of her crying, and the passage says the one grieving keeps calling out day after day.
notes.AS30: This passage is about what a person says, whether behind someone's back or as sharp words to their face, and it asks whether those words are true and beneficial. That bears on how your manager speaks when she calls out your mistakes before the whole office. It says nothing about whether to push through or leave, so it doesn't answer that part of your question.
notes.AS34: The passage speaks to the part of what you wrote about leaving and the fear of having no job. It describes someone who keeps turning to count how much they can carry out with them, and says that this counting means they "will never find a way out." It says no one swims ashore with their baggage, though it doesn't say how people manage the crossing, and it says nothing about a family's needs.
notes.AS39: The passage opens on the same thing you describe: money wringing tears out of a person. It speaks of the worry that comes with money and the sorrow over losses that weigh heavier than they seem. It says nothing about debt or about doing things right, so it meets only the crying and the weight of watching money go.
notes.AS45: The passage opens with "Be not afraid," which meets the fear you named head on. You wrote that you don't know if you can do this a second time, and the passage speaks to that sense of repeating: it says not to count how many times you fail, because time is infinite. It does not speak to the diagnosis itself, only to going forward again.
notes.AS57: The passage speaks to the last thing you wrote, about not deserving to feel alive. Seneca, in the passage, describes wanting to end his life and being held back by how little his father could bear losing him. He says he "commanded" himself to live, and calls living, at times, an act of bravery. It doesn't speak to the forgiving or the cheating itself.
notes.AS58: The passage speaks of a betrayal by someone trusted, a close friend who shared bread and then turned against the speaker. It names the harm as coming from the friend's act, which fits the part of your words where someone you trusted crossed a boundary. It says nothing about the speaker having encouraged it, so it doesn't speak to the going-over in your head.
notes.AS61: The passage tells of Abram being asked to leave his country, his relatives and his father's house for a land not yet shown to him. That meets the part of your situation where a move abroad means leaving the familiar behind, and where the destination is still unknown. It says nothing about whether a job is the right choice in the long run, so on that question it gives no answer.
notes.AS63: The passage speaks to the gap you describe between how others see you and how you see yourself. It says that when others think you are "somebody," you should distrust yourself, and that wanting to seem knowledgeable pulls attention away from improving. It says nothing about the fear of being seen through, only about the weight put on appearances.
notes.AS66: The passage describes a heart that has grown tired and cries out to God, asking why He makes Himself "so scarce" and doesn't come to speak for Himself. That meets the part of what you wrote about not having felt God in a long time, despite Mass and daily prayer. It doesn't say anything about doing something wrong; it only gives the cry itself.
notes.AS69: The passage speaks to the part of what you wrote about goals that have gone flat. It says principles die only when the thoughts behind them go out, and that those thoughts can be fanned back into flame. For returning to everyday life, it points to one way: "look at things again as thou didst use to look at them," which it calls recovering your life.
notes.AS76: The passage is about sleeping without fear, and about lying down full of sympathy for all living creatures. Your dog resting his head on your knee in sleep is a small picture of that, a creature lying down untroubled in your presence. The passage doesn't speak to the fullness in your heart directly, but its last line, about kindness toward every living being, is close to it.
notes.H03: The passage speaks of plans broken off and the heart's hopes ending, and that fits what you describe: a future you had pictured with her, cut short without warning, and fear about what comes next now that you are without a partner. It doesn't speak to the anger or to your questions about fault; it stays with the loss of what was planned.
notes.H06: The passage speaks to the part of your letter about this one door closing. It says a first failure leads many to lose heart, yet the person who keeps trying, and doesn't postpone his life, has "a hundred chances" rather than one. It doesn't speak to the sadness itself, only to how much one outcome is made to hold.
notes.H07: The passage is Augustine writing about losing a close friend, and it gives the same weight to absence that you give to yours. He says home became a torment and every place was hated for lacking the one he'd shared it with. Your dog was your reason to come home each day, and the passage speaks to that emptied place. It stays with the loss and offers no way out of it.
notes.H08: The passage speaks only to the part of your situation about your children and what a life leaves behind. It says some children justify a life and some are only regrets, which is close to the grudge you describe fearing, where time given to them gets weighed against what you wanted to achieve. It says nothing about how to choose between career and parenting.
notes.H10: The passage speaks to the part of this that is about handles: each way you've described meeting your mother, in speech, in silence and in distance, seems to leave you holding something heavy. It says a thing can be carried by one handle and not by the other, and that the unbearable handle is the wrong she does. Its counsel is to take hold of the bond instead, that she is your mother. It doesn't say whether a way out exists.
notes.H12: The passage says that once you isolate yourself, everything hurts, and that feeling for others brings help. That speaks to the ache of being alone with your own thoughts all the time. It doesn't speak to the reaching out that always ends badly; on that, the passage says nothing.
notes.H14: The passage speaks to one side of your bind: the weight of betraying your friend's confidence. It says that revealing a friend's secrets lets him go like a bird from the hand, and that unlike a wound or an insult, this leaves "no hope" of return. It doesn't speak to your care for his wife or to what she is owed, so that half of your dilemma goes unaddressed here.
notes.H15: The passage speaks most directly to the belittling and to being kept at your level. It says "he who does the lower work is not therefore a lower man," and that people are judged by the manner and spirit of their work, not by the position they hold. So the standing your boss gives you, or withholds, is not the measure the passage uses. It says nothing about bosses or credit-taking, so it doesn't reach the rest of what you described.
notes.H16: The passage is spoken by an older man looking at his own years, and it speaks to the part of what you wrote about unmet wants. He says he no longer desires what he did as a boy, and he proposes ceasing to desire what we have long desired. As for time running short, he lives each day as a complete life, one that might even be his last, though he does not snatch at it.
notes.H18: The passage meets your question about the point of it all by agreeing that death comes to everyone, and it says we are always watching people die around us. What it disputes is the idea that this life is the goal, which it calls a mistake, saying the world is "a means to an end." So where you see running toward an unknown goal that ends in death, the passage says the end lies beyond this life.
notes.H19: You describe so much darkness around you: war, fire, cruelty, poverty. The passage speaks to how one meets it, saying that crying out "it is dark" does not make darkness leave, while bringing in light makes it vanish at once. It does not say how to keep the darkness from creeping into you; it speaks only of light as what answers darkness.
notes.H20: The passage says what counts is not the outward habit but whether the virtues are actually practised and the will is truly given over. That speaks to your worry about converting only for appearance's sake: the passage puts weight on what is inwardly real, not on the outward form. It says nothing about whether he should ask this of you, or about accepting you as you are.
notes.H21: The passage names the exact wound you describe: someone close, someone trusted, who turns against you. It speaks of a friend "who ate bread with me," a person let into the ordinary, private parts of life. It doesn't answer your question of why she did it, but it does say that a betrayal from a close friend is a real and painful kind.
notes.H22: The passage takes up the part of what you wrote about people behaving at odds with what is preached. It says the speaker would never last five minutes in church if he left at every false sentiment, and that the street is just as false. It adds that even in his own manners and speech, the lie remains.
notes.H24: The passage speaks to the part of what you wrote about how you see your body and face. It says the mind and body are bound together, and that "disappointment" and "despondency" show up in the body's health and grace. It does not say you are ugly or beautiful. Its focus is the mind behind the face, not the comparison with others.
notes.H25: The passage is about money, but its point is that people measure others by their own yardstick, and what grips one person barely touches another. It speaks to the comment that broke your heart: the passage asks why one person's standard should be used to judge someone else. It says nothing about weight, eating, or the spiral itself.
notes.H28: The passage describes two ways a parent can stand with a child: stepping into his place so that both see the same thing, or looking in from outside and guessing at his situation before giving orders. It says the second way never wins obedience. You wrote that you wanted to prepare him for the world, and this passage speaks to that part, about how a parent's aim reaches a child, not about whether the aim was good.
notes.H29: The passage is about someone being preferred over another, so it fits the part of your story that involves your wife's career, not your promotion. It says that if such advancement is good, one ought to rejoice for the person who gets it, and if it is bad, not to grieve at missing it. What lies behind her "Oh, that's nice" is something the passage doesn't speak to.
notes.H30: The passage separates a bare fact from the judgment added to it, and it says the trouble lies in that judgment, so "we must not get rid of poverty, but of the opinion about poverty." You spent your life getting rid of the poverty itself, and the passage points to something else as the thing to be rid of. It speaks to the anger you describe, not to what to do next.
notes.H32: The passage describes a long wait that ends in something small: a smile and talk about nothing, and the sense that this was what the waiting had been for. That speaks to what you wrote about hoping for years and finally finding someone. It doesn't say anything about the engagement itself, only about the moment when the long wait feels answered.
